title: Markets Turn on the AI Buildout, Iran Talks Stall on Sequencing, Two Senate Seats Still Open
bluf: The Iran war is still the defining factor. Three more tankers were damaged near Qatar on November 5, Trump said he may have to destroy the rest of the country, and a carrier group is heading to the region, while Qatar shuttles a plan that trades lifting the blockade and IAEA access for reopening Hormuz. Wall Street had its worst day in years: the Nasdaq fell 5.5% and the Nasdaq 100 6.4%, its worst session since March 2020, on fears that a Democratic Congress slows the AI buildout; futures point to a partial rebound this morning. Democrats hold 54 Senate seats with Mississippi (a margin of about 138 votes) and Alaska (ranked choice tally November 18) still open, and a Justice Department suit over a second Dan Sullivan on the Alaska ballot is the main certification risk. In Cuba, Yoani Sánchez was released after more than nine hours, but two other independent journalists remain jailed and the Law 186 government overhaul takes effect November 9. Ukraine talks move to Abu Dhabi November 10 to 11 after a White House event marking the Oleshky humanitarian truce.
coverageNote: Built the morning of November 6 from wire roundups, regional outlets and official releases collected overnight. Market closing figures come from wire reports collected the evening of November 5. The headlines table lists leading coverage collected this cycle, not print front pages.

worldConditions.overall: Global risk stays high. The US and Iran remain at war with Hormuz traffic restricted, and diplomacy is stuck on sequencing: Tehran wants the blockade and sanctions lifted first, Washington wants the nuclear file up front. A sharp equity selloff adds a financial stress channel to an already strained picture, and the US transition of power in Congress is moving through two close Senate counts and a federal lawsuit.
worldConditions.postureBasis: Active US and Iran hostilities with weekly tanker damage; no ceasefire mechanism agreed; Russia and Ukraine still fighting with talks scheduled; a hybrid campaign against European infrastructure without attribution; market volatility not seen since 2020.

updates.update: Three more tankers damaged November 5 and UKMTO reported a tanker hit by two projectiles 50 nautical miles north of Madinat ash Shamal, Qatar. Trump met his national security team and said Iran would know soon enough; the NYT reports US forces are poised to resume major combat. Iran sent a nuclear proposal via Qatar to be discussed only after the US meets seven demands.

Democrats hold 54 seats. Mississippi is within about 138 votes with roughly 3,600 mail ballots left and certification due November 13; Alaska ranked choice results come November 18 while a DOJ suit seeks to block certification if Peltola wins.

Melania Trump hosted Russian and Ukrainian delegations (Dmitriev and Arakhamia) at the White House to mark the Oleshky truce; more than 750 people were evacuated and Russia refused an extension. Trump met Dmitriev and predicted a deal soon. Abu Dhabi talks are set for November 10 to 11.

Yoani Sánchez was released after more than nine hours. Adelth Bonne Gamboa of CubaNet (arrested November 2) and Henry Constantín (jailed since September 16) remain held; RSF, IAPA and Amnesty condemned the detentions. Law 186 was gazetted November 2 and takes effect November 9.

Still no attribution for the supermarket refrigeration hacks. Belgium opened a prosecution and the EU called the attacks deliberate; the flaws in Danfoss and Copeland controllers were disclosed in August and about 13,000 systems were exposed online.
No verified November activity figures collected; the story stays steady pending fresh MND data.
No new legal or street challenges found. Inauguration remains January 1.

items.headline: Two Senate races still open
items.summary: Democrats hold 54 seats and flipped Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Ohio, North Carolina, South Carolina and Texas. In Mississippi, Democrat Scott Colom leads Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith 49.0% to 48.9% with about 3,600 mail ballots left; certification is due November 13. In Alaska, Mary Peltola leads Sen. Dan Sullivan 48.2% to 47.9% with ranked choice results due November 18.
items.source: NBC and Fox counts via wire roundups
items.assessment: A Mississippi Democratic win would be the first since 1982; expect recount requests in both races.

items.headline: DOJ suit could stall Alaska certification
items.summary: The Justice Department sued in October to block certification if Peltola wins by less than the vote total of a second, unaffiliated candidate named Daniel J. Sullivan, arguing voters may have been confused. Trump said he ordered the suit and has urged prosecuting Peltola. Legal scholars say the statute does not let DOJ enjoin a state certification.

items.headline: Judge pauses the Trump arch; LA picks a new mayor
items.summary: A federal judge blocked construction of the planned arch for 14 days. In Los Angeles, Nithya Raman defeated Mayor Karen Bass. In California, Gov. Newsom commuted 548 death sentences.

items.headline: More tankers hit; Trump weighs a heavier strike
items.summary: The IRGC said three more tankers were damaged November 5, two by mines and one by fire. UKMTO reported a tanker hit by two projectiles 50 nautical miles north of Madinat ash Shamal, Qatar. Trump said he would rather not destroy the rest of the country but may have to, met his national security team, and spoke with the Qatari emir, who urged restraint. A carrier group is heading to the region via Singapore.
items.assessment: We assess renewed large scale US strikes within two weeks are roughly even odds; the carrier movement and public threats point up, the Qatari channel points down.

items.headline: Diplomacy stuck on sequencing
items.summary: Iran sent a nuclear proposal through Qatar that it will discuss only after the US meets seven demands, including lifting sanctions and paying war reparations. A Qatari draft reported by Axios has the US lift the blockade and release some frozen funds and Iran invite the IAEA to bombed sites on day one, with Hormuz reopening on day two and nuclear talks on the enriched uranium stockpile after that. Iranian sources told Reuters another US attack is more likely than a deal.
items.source: Reuters via ROIC; Axios; Iran International

items.headline: Tehran leans on the region
items.summary: Foreign Minister Araghchi called his counterparts in the UAE, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, Pakistan, Oman and Egypt. Parliament speaker Qalibaf mocked Vice President Vance as a losing gambler after Vance blamed the war for the midterm losses.
items.source: Iranian state media, labeled as claims; wire roundups

items.headline: Israel: Herzog weighs who forms the next government
items.summary: After the October 27 election left Netanyahu's bloc at 53 seats and Gadi Eisenkot's at 48, President Herzog began consultations, meeting the smallest parties first. Eisenkot was expected to have more endorsements than Netanyahu. The election commission reviewed 9,069 polling stations and found no fraud.
items.assessment: The mandate decision is expected between now and next Tuesday; Arab party endorsements could decide it.

items.headline: White House marks the Oleshky truce
items.summary: Melania Trump hosted Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev and Ukraine's David Arakhamia to mark the six day humanitarian ceasefire in occupied Oleshky (October 27 to November 1). More than 750 people were evacuated; Russia refused to extend it. President Trump met Dmitriev but not the Ukrainians and predicted a deal soon.

items.headline: Abu Dhabi talks next week
items.summary: Witkoff and Kushner lead the US side at three way talks in Abu Dhabi November 10 to 11. German Chancellor Merz hosts a coalition of the willing summit November 19. Russia holds about 80% of Donetsk.

items.headline: Yoani Sánchez released; two journalists still held
items.summary: Yoani Sánchez, director of 14ymedio, was released after more than nine hours in custody. Adelth Bonne Gamboa of CubaNet, arrested November 2, and Henry Constantín, jailed since September 16, remain detained. RSF, the Inter American Press Association and Amnesty International condemned the detentions.

items.headline: Law 186 reshapes the government from November 9
items.summary: The law, approved July 30 and published November 2 in the Gaceta Oficial, cuts the cabinet to 20 ministries plus the Central Bank and merges Commerce, Construction and Agriculture into fewer bodies. Officials present it as streamlining; critics see a shuffle that leaves the economic model untouched.

items.headline: Pope Leo begins South America tour
items.summary: The first US born pope is in Uruguay November 6 to 8, Argentina November 8 to 11 and Peru November 11 to 17, about 50 events in 10 cities, including a return to Chiclayo, where he was bishop, and a meeting with President Milei.

items.headline: Former FBI agent charged
items.summary: DOJ charged former FBI agent Andrew Reyes on November 5. Details of the charges were not collected this cycle.

items.headline: Election claims fade, Alaska suit gives them a new hook
items.summary: Rigging claims about the midterms have lost momentum as most losers conceded, but the DOJ suit over the second Dan Sullivan gives the "stolen seat" framing a new focus in Alaska.

items.headline: Fridge hacks: still no attribution
items.summary: No group has claimed or been named for the attacks on supermarket refrigeration controllers. Belgium opened a prosecution and the EU called them deliberate. The Danfoss and Copeland flaws were disclosed by Claroty August 9; Forescout counted about 13,000 exposed systems. The Pentagon is reviewing August freezer failures at military commissaries.
items.assessment: Attribution to a state actor is unlikely to be public within a week; the Pentagon review is the signpost for a US angle.

items.headline: Mexican judge arrested in Ryan Wedding case
items.summary: A Mexican judge was arrested over an alleged $2 million bribe tied to the case against Ryan Wedding, the former Olympic snowboarder accused of running a cocaine network and ordering the killing of a federal witness. Wedding was captured in Mexico in January.

items.headline: Why the doomsday date keeps spreading
items.summary: Writers revisiting the 1960 "Doomsday" paper note that a specific date, a real scientific source and a Friday the 13th make a claim shareable. The historian Alan MacEachern argues the lesson is about how confidently findings are presented.

items.headline: AI selloff after the election
items.summary: Nvidia fell 9.2%, about $440 billion in value, and the largest tech stocks lost more than $1 trillion as investors priced in a Congress that may slow data center and chip spending. South Korea's Kospi fell about 8 to 9% and halted trading.
items.assessment: The move reflects policy risk pricing, not new data on AI demand; a rebound is likely if Democratic leaders signal support for the buildout.

items.headline: Google: accept AI or lose Search in schools
items.summary: From early 2027, Gemini and Search will be off by default on K-12 student accounts; schools that switch AI off entirely will also lose Search. Fairplay urged schools to consider other search engines.

items.headline: Claim: a scientist said the world ends November 13
items.summary: The date comes from a real 1960 Science paper. Its authors fitted a curve to population history that reached infinity in late 2026, and they picked Friday the 13th partly as a joke. Population growth peaked soon after and the curve stopped matching reality.

items.summary: More than 750 civilians left the occupied town during the six day truce, the largest humanitarian pause of the war in that area.

conspiracies.claim: The midterms were rigged through fake ballots and compromised machines
conspiracies.status: Fading, with a new Alaska focus
conspiracies.whereSpreading: X first, then other platforms. NewsGuard had logged 55 viral midterm claims by November 5, 26 about fraud, 29 of them starting on X.
conspiracies.origin: Recycled from 2020 narratives about Dominion and foreign made machines, plus new claims such as an FBI Houston raid that supposedly found fraudulent ballots on November 2.
conspiracies.whyBelieved: It offers a ready explanation for a loss, builds on years of repetition, and links real Election Day problems into a larger pattern.
conspiracies.caseFor: Believers point to real Election Day problems such as long lines and machine errors, documented individual cases of voter fraud, foreign made components in voting equipment, and distrust of mail ballots.
conspiracies.caseAgainst: FBI Houston said the claimed raid never happened. NewsGuard found no credible source for a supposed Dominion whistleblower. Individual fraud cases are prosecuted but have not been shown to change outcomes, and even prominent former election deniers largely conceded this time.
conspiracies.unknowns: Mississippi is within about 138 votes with mail ballots still out, and Alaska results depend on ranked choice tabulation November 18 and a DOJ suit over a second Dan Sullivan on the ballot. Either could revive claims from one side or the other.
conspiracies.watch: Recount requests in Mississippi; the court's ruling on the DOJ Alaska suit; whether any losing candidate refuses to concede.

conspiracies.claim: Democrats won by importing foreigners and registering them to vote (Great Replacement framing)
conspiracies.whereSpreading: Prominent right wing accounts on X, Gab and Telegram in the 48 hours after the vote.
conspiracies.origin: The Great Replacement theory, recast to explain the election result.
conspiracies.whyBelieved: It explains a defeat as something done to voters rather than a choice they made, and taps into immigration anxiety already high during the deportation campaign.
conspiracies.caseFor: Supporters point to high immigration levels in recent years, a strong swing among Latino voters, and Democratic support for immigrant friendly policies.
conspiracies.caseAgainst: Noncitizens cannot legally vote in federal elections, and no evidence of mass noncitizen registration has been produced. Post election analysis, including CFR's, and statements by Vance and Trump tie the result to the Iran war, gas prices and cost of living. Rep. Salazar said Hispanic voters punished indiscriminate deportations, which points to citizens changing their votes.
conspiracies.unknowns: Voter file studies of exactly who switched sides will take months.
conspiracies.watch: This theory has motivated mass casualty attacks before. Watch for calls to violence and for targeting of immigrant communities and election workers.

conspiracies.claim: Ebola is a hoax, a Western bioweapon, or a scheme for aid groups to make money
conspiracies.whereSpreading: Community networks in eastern DRC, French language TikTok, and Western anti vaccine and supplement seller accounts.
conspiracies.origin: Long standing distrust from earlier outbreaks and conflict, plus lab origin and planned pandemic narratives that took off online after WHO's May 17 emergency declaration.
conspiracies.whyBelieved: Decades of conflict, distrust of government and foreign responders, and the fact that no approved vaccine existed for this Bundibugyo strain make official messaging easy to doubt.
conspiracies.caseFor: Believers cite the history of unethical foreign medical experiments in Africa, large aid budgets flowing into outbreak zones, the lack of an approved vaccine for this strain, and repeated outbreaks in the same regions.
conspiracies.caseAgainst: More than 5,300 people have died since May, mostly in the DRC, and the strain kills about half of those infected. Health workers have documented the cases, and rumors have led residents to burn treatment tents, including an MSF isolation tent in Mongbwalu, and to hide sick relatives.
conspiracies.unknowns: How the first human infection in this outbreak happened was not established in the reporting reviewed for this edition.
conspiracies.watch: Rumors about the two new vaccine trials, which are likely to become the next target.

sources.title: KAS: Health disinformation and the Ebola outbreak

conspiracies.claim: A scientist predicted the world ends on Friday, November 13, 2026
conspiracies.whereSpreading: Viral headlines and short videos, plus mainstream explainers: The Conversation (republished by Gizmodo and ScienceDaily), Futura Sciences and South Asian news sites ran pieces from mid October.
conspiracies.origin: A 1960 scientific paper on population growth whose model reached a mathematical infinity around that date.
conspiracies.whyBelieved: A specific date, a real scientific source and a Friday the 13th make it shareable, and it lands in a stressful news cycle.
conspiracies.caseFor: The date traces back to a real, peer reviewed 1960 paper in Science by Heinz von Foerster and two colleagues. Their curve matched world population closely for decades, and some writers note that if current trends broke down suddenly the paper's broader warning about strain on resources would still matter.
conspiracies.caseAgainst: The authors said the model would blow up at that point only if growth kept accelerating, and picked Friday the 13th partly as a joke. Growth rates peaked in the 1960s, the curve stopped fitting by the early 1990s, world population is about 8 billion, and UN projections show a peak around 10.3 billion in the 2080s.
conspiracies.watch: Scam and engagement bait pages using the date around November 13.
conspiracies.unknowns: How much attention the date draws in the final week, and whether scam or engagement bait pages use it.

discourse.summary: The post election information space is dominated by authentic domestic argument over why Republicans lost: the war (Vance's framing), replacement and fraud theories on the far right, and a visible break between some extremist networks and Trump. Foreign influence operations were active before the vote, and their likely next move is to reframe the result as American defeat and division. No coordinated campaign has yet been tied to the European bomb threats.

corrections.text: Lula's fourth term begins January 5, 2027, not January 1 as this edition and Edition 001 said. A 2021 constitutional amendment moved the inauguration date. Forecast f005, which used the wrong date, is voided and replaced by f008.

Flávio Bolsonaro did not hand over his passports. He missed the Supreme Court deadline, police canceled the passports on October 27, and he landed in Miami on October 28 via Argentina. The Brazil story file has been corrected.

This edition said Adelth Bonne Gamboa remains detained. Diario de Cuba reported a violent arrest on November 2 with threats, a fine and seized equipment; whether he is still in custody is not confirmed.
